description: How a finding becomes a work item in Azure DevOps. Generates the publisher, the backlog preview on screen and the backlog workbook, so the thing exported, the thing approved and the thing created are the same thing built once.

auth.patNote: Supported because most clients will hand over a token before they will register an application. Stored in Key Vault, never in the database, and the product records its expiry and warns before it lapses rather than failing a publish on a Friday.

processTemplates.description: Field names differ by process. The publisher reads the project's process before writing and maps to what exists, rather than assuming Agile.
processTemplates.unsupportedBehaviour: A custom process with renamed fields is detected by reading the work item type definition. Fields that do not exist are left unset and reported, rather than failing the whole publish on one missing field.

grouping.description: One work item per finding would produce four hundred tasks nobody will ever groom. One per rule loses the evidence. The grouping below is what a consultant would have done by hand.

epic.title: {categoryName}
epic.when: Always, for any category with at least one finding that has an estimate.
epic.note: Categories rather than domains, because a sprint is planned around kinds of work rather than around parts of the platform.

feature.title: {ruleName}
feature.when: A rule with more than three findings, or any rule whose work item type is epic.
feature.note: The feature carries the rule's explanation once, so the stories under it do not repeat it forty times.

story.title: {ruleName}: {componentName}
story.when: The rule's work item type is story or bug.
story.note: One named component per story. This is the level at which somebody can pick it up on a Tuesday and finish it.

task.title: {ruleName} ({count} components)
task.when: The rule's work item type is task. Trivial findings are grouped: twenty missing descriptions is one task, not twenty.
task.note: The individual components are listed in the description so nothing is lost, and the count is in the title so nobody is surprised by what they picked up.

fields.System.Title: From the grouping template above. Truncated at 255 characters with the component name preserved rather than the rule name, because the component is what makes it findable.
fields.System.Description: Built from the finding: what was found, on which component, in which solution, with the evidence. Then why it matters, from the rule. Then the modernisation options where the rule has them, including the case for leaving it alone. HTML, because that is what the field renders.
fields.Microsoft.VSTS.Common.AcceptanceCriteria: From the rule's acceptance criteria template, with the component substituted in. Always present. A work item generated by a tool with no acceptance criteria is a work item that gets closed by somebody deciding it was fine.
fields.Microsoft.VSTS.Scheduling.StoryPoints: The approved story points. Omitted on task and bug types where the process does not carry the field.
fields.Microsoft.VSTS.Scheduling.OriginalEstima: The midpoint of the approved range, in hours, because the field holds one number. The range itself goes in the description with its rationale, so the number in the field is never the only record of it.
fields.Microsoft.VSTS.Common.Priority: Mapped from severity: critical to 1, high to 2, medium to 3, low and info to 4.
fields.System.Tags: A fixed set so a client can filter to this tool's output and delete it wholesale if they decide not to proceed: the product tag, the engagement name, the rule id, the category, the severity, the component type, and where an estimate came from.
fields.System.AreaPath: From the engagement configuration. Defaults to the project root.
fields.System.IterationPath: From the engagement configuration. Defaults to the project root, never to the current sprint. Dropping forty items into an active sprint is not a thing to do to somebody by default.

descriptionSections.description: Fixed order. A reader who has seen one of these has seen them all, which is the point.

order.heading: What was found
order.content: The component, its solution, and the attribute values that triggered the rule.

order.heading: Evidence
order.content: The raw values, so somebody can check the claim rather than take it. A recommendation nobody can verify is one nobody will act on.

order.heading: Why it matters
order.content: From the rule. The same sentence every time for the same rule, deliberately.

order.heading: Options
order.content: From the modernisation map where the rule points at one, each with what it gains and what it costs, and the case for leaving it alone.

order.heading: Estimate
order.content: The range, the confidence, the rationale and the assumptions. Where the estimate came from a model rather than a person, it says so in the same sentence.

order.heading: Provenance
order.content: The run, the date, the extraction mode and the identity it ran as. Whoever reads this in six months needs to know how much to trust it.

acceptanceCriteria.description: Owned by acceptance-criteria.json, one entry per rule that produces a work item. Not generated per finding: the criterion is a property of the rule, and the component is substituted into it at publish time.
acceptanceCriteria.fallback: There is none. A rule with no criterion fails the contract check and never reaches a publish, because a generated work item whose acceptance criterion is boilerplate teaches a team to close the rest without reading them.

identity.description: What makes a publish idempotent, and what lets a second run update rather than duplicate.
identity.key: A deterministic identifier derived from the engagement id, the rule id and the stable component key. Written into a tag and into a custom field where the project has one.

onSecondPublish.stillFound: Update the estimate, the description and the evidence. Never reopen a closed item: somebody closed it for a reason and this tool does not know what it was.
onSecondPublish.noLongerFound: Add a comment saying the finding is gone and which run found it gone. Never close the item automatically. Closing somebody's work item because a tool could not see the problem any more is not a thing to do without a person.
onSecondPublish.newFinding: Create it, in the same epic and feature as its siblings.

safety.dryRun: Always available and always the default on the first publish against a project. Produces exactly what would be created, as the backlog workbook, without calling the API.
safety.limit: A publish creating more than two hundred work items requires a second confirmation naming the count. Nobody means to put nine hundred items in somebody's backlog.
safety.record: Every created and updated item is recorded with its identifier and URL, so a publish that went into the wrong project can be found and removed rather than hunted.
